analysis.one_liner: Bans forced-arbitration and class-action-waiver clauses in consumer financial contracts, letting customers sue banks and lenders in court.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Nearly every bank, credit card, and lending contract contains a clause requiring customers to settle disputes in private arbitration and forbidding them from joining class-action lawsuits. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable for consumer financial products, so consumers could take complaints about fees, billing, or lending practices to a judge and could band together in class actions. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with bank accounts, credit cards, loans, and other financial products. They regain the ability to sue in court over fees, wrongful collections, or discrimination, and to join class actions—currently the only realistic remedy when individual losses are too small to litigate alone.

how_it_helps.text: Makes any agreement to arbitrate a future consumer financial dispute invalid and unenforceable, so consumers could sue in court instead.
Void waivers that bar consumers from joining class actions, restoring the main practical remedy for small-dollar financial harm.
Requires a court, not an arbitrator, to decide whether the law applies, closing a common loophole where companies delegate the question to the arbitrator.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, lenders, and other consumer financial companies, which would face lawsuits and class actions they currently avoid through arbitration clauses; some litigation costs could be passed to customers.

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue that class-action litigation is slow and expensive, and that arbitration is a faster, cheaper way to resolve individual disputes; the bill removes companies' ability to steer all disputes into that channel.
The bill applies only to consumer financial products and disputes arising after enactment, so consumers with existing contracts and pending disputes would not benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—restoring consumers' practical ability to challenge wrongful fees and practices—is broad but hard to quantify; the cost is real but modest: financial companies would litigate some disputes in court rather than in cheaper, private arbitration, and businesses argue (in general debates over the Federal Arbitration Act) that class litigation is slower and more expensive. Given that only disputes that actually arise would be affected, and that consumers currently almost never win in individual arbitration, the public benefit likely outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, got no hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 3, 2022 and read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
No further action was taken; the bill never left committee and received no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill had 23 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, with no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial companies keep the arbitration clauses that prevent customers from banding together in court over fees and lending abuses.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as sponsor; chaired the Banking Committee, which nonetheless never took it up.

for.name: 23 senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Schatz, Warren, Sanders, Durbin, and Klobuchar.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents; no Republicans supported the bill, and the Republican-controlled-at-times Banking Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and consumer financial companies
industries.note: They would lose the ability to force disputes into private arbitration and to block class actions, making them easier to sue over fees, billing, and lending practices. Arbitration clauses currently shield small-dollar harms from any meaningful challenge.
Consumer arbitration is a fee-for-service business; banning predispute arbitration clauses in consumer finance would eliminate much of that business.
